transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-02
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Samantha Cho (Redwood AE), Miguel Alvarez (Redwood SE), Dr. Lina Park (CatalystOps), Omar Reyes (CatalystOps), Tara Singh (CatalystOps Security)

Summary (auto): Quick technical deep dive on long-context strategies for 128k+ use cases. Focused on sparse windowing, prefix chunking, KV persistence & warm/cold caching, quant tradeoffs, and on-prem constraints. Action items recorded.

Topics: sparse attention windows; prefix chunking + append strategies; persistent KV cache (disk-backed vs in-memory); batching and latency SLOs; int8 vs int4 quantization artifacts; multi-GPU sharding for ultra-long seqs; VPC onboarding notes.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Samantha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. um we wanna dig into CatalystOps long context workflow, so Lina could you kick off with your current constraints?
[00:00:18] Dr. Lina: Sure, hi, thanks. we ingest compliance docs, medical notes, and long transcripts — typical doc slices are 10k to 60k tokens but we want a single-session view, so target is 128k to 512k for research. latency SLO is 300ms p95 for short queries, but for the long retrieval flows we can accept 2-5s. main ask is predictable throughput and not blowing up cost.
[00:00:45] Miguel: Right, ok, predictable cost is key. are you currently using a vector DB or are you doing append and streaming?
[00:00:52] Omar: we do hybrid — vector DB for retrieval, then append top-k chunks into a single prompt. but the problem is the tokenized size plus the KV cache blow out on GPU memory, so we want to explore prefix chunking and sparse attention windows.
[00:01:12] Samantha: perfect, we'll walk through three patterns we recommend: 1) sliding-prefetch + append (short-lived KV), 2) hierarchical chunking with summarize-then-append, 3) mounted-context / persistent KV where KV is paged to NVMe and hot sets kept in GPU. each has latency/cost tradeoffs.
[00:01:35] [Speaker 2]: (mumble) can you write that down?
[00:01:40] Miguel: yeah, so pattern A: sliding prefetch — you keep a moving window of the last N tokens in GPU KV, evict older keys. this is low-latency for recency queries but costs more network calls if you need to refill and you lose global document view. for 128k windows, we typically recommend chunking to 16k-32k and stitching with sparse attention.
[00:02:05] Dr. Lina: stitching how? like placeholder tokens?
[00:02:10] Miguel: two approaches: prefix-chunk append where you include chunk heads with dense attention and rest with sparse-attention masks (so attention matrix is banded), or hierarchical: compute chunk embeddings, run a brief summary model per chunk then send summaries plus a few exact chunks. the former preserves token-level context but is heavier.
[00:02:32] Omar: we prefer not to summarize aggressively because medical accuracy suffers. can you explain the banded attention thing more?
[00:02:40] Miguel: sure — imagine attention window size W applied locally (e.g., 4k), and we add a sparse global token set — chunk anchors — that every chunk attends to. that reduces full O(L^2) to O(L*W + G*L) depending on G anchors. it's similar to BigBird/Longformer patterns. kernel selection matters — some runtimes support sparse kernels natively, others emulate with block-sparse matmul.
[00:03:10] Tara: how reliable is block-sparse on GPUs? we worry about perf cliffs.
[00:03:16] Miguel: good point — block-sparse implementations can be brittle. Redwood's runtime will choose between three execution paths based on sequence profile: dense kernel with tiling for small to mid seqs, streaming multi-pass for extreme lengths, or block-sparse when the model/adapter supports it. in our experience on Ampere/Blackwell GPUs, block-sparse gives good throughput only when anchor density is low and blocks align to memory pages. misaligned blocks cause bank conflicts and drop perf.
[00:03:49] [00:03:52] Dr. Lina: you mentioned persistent KV — what is the cost of persisting KV to NVMe and paging into GPU?
[00:03:58] Miguel: NVMe-backed KV works well for very long contexts. Redwood implements tiered KV: L0 = GPU resident hot rows, L1 = remote network cache (shared pool), L2 = NVMe snapshot. Cold pages paged in asynchronously; worst-case page fault causes 10s-100s ms penalty depending on IO and network. to hit your 2-5s tolerance for long queries that's usually fine, but for 300ms SLO it's unacceptable unless your hotset is warm.
[00:04:28] Omar: what about concurrent request patterns? We have spikes when multiple analysts query same cases.
[00:04:33] Miguel: that's where prefix dedup and shared KV helps. Redwood can shard KV by document and reuse anchors across queries. Also batching policy — continuous batching helps throughput but increases tail latency. for tight p95 we use smaller max batch sizes and prefer async pre-warm of KV.
[00:04:54] Samantha: quick question: what's your on-prem footprint? single rack? multi-region VPC?
[00:04:59] Omar: single private cluster for now, 8x H100s, 3x control nodes. we want private control plane with KMS integration.
[00:05:10] Miguel: perfect — on-prem gives us direct NVMe and local network which helps KV paging. main caveat: GPU memory fragmentation and CUDA context switching can still cause increased latency for long KV loads; we recommend pinned-memory strategies and small process pools instead of one giant process creating new contexts per request.
[00:05:32] Dr. Lina: on quantization: we tried int8 and got hallucination increases. can you walk us through the tradeoffs for int4/int8 for these long contexts?
[00:05:40] Miguel: absolutely. int8 often preserves logits better but costs more memory than int4. int4 reduces memory footprint ~2x vs int8, but can introduce distribution shifts in attention scaling and rotary embedding interpolation, especially for long positions. Redwood's Optimize tool runs calibration with representative context lengths — mixing FP16 for attention layers and int4 for FFN is a common hybrid. also per-channel scaling and bias correction helps.
[00:06:10] Tara: curious — do you support symmetric quant or per-channel? we need deterministic outputs for audits.
[00:06:15] Miguel: we support per-channel quant and post-calibration bias correction. determinism depends on kernel choices; certain fused int4 kernels are non-deterministic across runs and GPUs. for audit purposes we can pin to deterministic kernels at the cost of perf.
[00:06:33] [00:06:36] Dr. Lina: how about streaming large outputs — we want partial answers while the rest loads, is that feasible?
[00:06:42] Samantha: yes, prefix streaming is an option: emit tokens from local window while remote pages are fetched; also Redwood supports partial-hypothesis scoring where top-k from hotset is emitted with a continuation token. UX caveat: coherence on streaming long documents can be tricky — you get early answers that may change after context fully loaded.
[00:07:05] Omar: can we run a pilot that keeps a 128k working set warm and measure p95?
[00:07:10] Miguel: yes — our suggested pilot: 1) Redwood runs a baseline 128k run on your sample prompts with mounted NVMe + hotset 32k, 2) try block-sparse anchors with 4k local windows, 3) run hybrid quant (int4 FFN + fp16 attn). we'll collect per-token latency, KV miss rates, GPU memory breakdown, and token generation cost.
[00:07:36] Samantha: I'll send the benchmark template and pricing follow-up.
[00:07:40] [00:07:42] Dr. Lina: what about security — SSO and KMS for keys, audit logs?
[00:07:47] Tara: (speaking) this is Tara — we need HSM integration and immutable audit logs for model input retention policy.
[00:07:54] Samantha: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and audit log forwarding. on-prem deployment can mount your HSM via PKCS11 and we ship audit hooks. we'll share the SOC2 docs and the integration notes.
[00:08:09] Miguel: also note network egress. if KV pages go out to remote cache, you need secured channels and private peering; otherwise use local NVMe to avoid egress.
[00:08:21] Omar: a couple of micro questions: 1) how does tokenization alignment affect chunk boundaries? 2) eviction policy — LRU or cost-based?
[00:08:29] Miguel: for chunk boundaries, align to semantic sentence boundaries if possible, but tokenization artifacts can split tokens. Redwood recommends a tokenizer-aware chunker that preserves whole tokens and prefers chunk heads at sentence starts so anchor tokens are meaningful. eviction: we use a cost-based policy (hotness score = access freq * recency weight * compute cost to rehydrate) which outperforms plain LRU for heavy compute docs.
[00:08:54] [00:09:00] Dr. Lina: any quick wins we can take now before pilot?
[00:09:03] Miguel: yes — 1) reduce sequence length by removing boilerplate with heuristics (regex and simple summarizer), 2) warm KV for nightly heavy cases, 3) use hybrid quantization and run calibration with your exact prompts.
[00:09:18] Samantha: we'll also send an implementation checklist for on-prem (KMS, NVMe layout, network peering, HSM certs).
[00:09:25] Miguel: last note on batching — continuous batching with dynamic timeouts helps amortize kernel launches; but if you need strict p95 you might cap batch size and enable immediate forwarding. there's no silver bullet.
[00:09:40] Omar: great, thanks this helps.
[00:09:44] [crosstalk] Dr. Lina: okay let's wrap with action items.

Recap / Action items (auto):
